name: Levellers
summary: The Levellers were a London and New Model Army movement of the late 1640s that demanded a written constitution placing supreme authority in a frequently elected Representative, a manhood franchise, equality before the law, jury trial, freedom of conscience, and an end to monopolies, tithes, excise and imprisonment for debt. They held that all just authority rests on the consent of the governed and that no Parliament may remove a short list of fundamental rights. They defended property and disclaimed any levelling of estates or common ownership without universal consent.

scope: The movement of 1646 to 1649 around Lilburne, Overton, Walwyn and Prince: its Agreements of the People (the 1649 text is used), the January 1648 petition, and the positions its spokesmen took at Putney in 1647. The True Levellers or Diggers (Winstanley), who wanted common ownership, are excluded, as are later radicals and modern movements that borrow the name.

missingStatements.text: No one should be punished for refusing to answer questions that would incriminate them.
missingStatements.rationale: The 1649 Agreement bars the Representative from punishing anyone for refusing to answer questions against themselves in criminal cases, and the 1648 petition protests committees imprisoning people for not answering interrogatories.

missingStatements.text: Legal proceedings should be conducted in the language ordinary people speak.
missingStatements.rationale: The Agreement allows no legal proceedings in any language but English, and the 1648 petition calls laws in French a badge of slavery and asks for them in the mother tongue.

notes: Themes searched: franchise and representation, property and levelling, tax, trade and monopolies, courts and criminal procedure, religion, army and conscription, the poor, press. Fuller texts of Overton, Walwyn and Lilburne were not reachable (Online Library of Liberty refused scripted access, HTTP 403; libertarianism.org returned 429), so economy, foreign affairs, family, ecology and identity themes remain unanswered and the record may fail the uncertainty rule. Answers rest only on words; the Levellers never held power. Women's franchise: the 1649 text says 'all men' without addressing women, so it stays null.
